items.stem: A study finds that towns with more ice-cream shops also have higher rates of sunburn. A columnist concludes that ice-cream shops cause sunburn. What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

choices.text: The sample size of towns studied was too small to be meaningful.
It mistakes a correlation for a causal relationship, ignoring a common cause (hot, sunny weather).
It assumes ice-cream shops are evenly distributed across all towns.
It fails to define what counts as an "ice-cream shop".

items.explanation: Both variables (ice-cream sales and sunburn) rise together because of a third factor — hot, sunny weather — which drives both. Neither causes the other. Two things moving together (correlating) does not mean one causes the other. Always ask: could a third, hidden variable be driving both? GAMSAT Section I loves burying this pattern in social-science stimulus about health, crime, education or the economy. Memory tip: Picture a puppeteer ("the third variable") standing behind two puppets (ice-cream sales and sunburn), pulling both their strings at once — the puppets never touch each other directly. Whenever two things move together, go looking for the puppeteer. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem: "To be eligible for the scholarship, an applicant must have a GPA above 3.5." A student has a GPA of 3.8 but was rejected for the scholarship. Which statement is best supported?

choices.text: The rule about GPA must be false.
A GPA above 3.5 is necessary but was not stated to be sufficient, so other criteria may also apply.
The student's GPA was calculated incorrectly.
The scholarship committee broke its own rule.

items.explanation: The original statement only establishes GPA as a minimum requirement (necessary), not as a guarantee of selection (sufficient). Rejection despite meeting the minimum is fully consistent with other unstated criteria existing. A necessary condition must be true for an outcome to happen ("you must have X"). A sufficient condition guarantees the outcome on its own ("having X is enough"). Confusing the two is one of the most common traps in GAMSAT Section I logic questions. Memory tip: N is a bouncer at the door: no ticket, no entry — but even with a ticket you might still be turned away for other reasons. S is a golden ticket that guarantees you get in, no questions asked. "Necessary = No entry without it, Sufficient = Ships you straight through." Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). items.stem: A passage opens by stating that public libraries are "the last truly free public space," then spends three paragraphs describing free wifi, warm shelter, and no obligation to buy anything. What is the main idea, and what are the paragraphs?

items.stem: "All fish live in water. A dolphin lives in water. Therefore, a dolphin is a fish." This argument is:

choices.text: Valid, because the conclusion follows the premises.
Invalid, because the premises do not logically guarantee the conclusion, even though the first premise is true.

Memory tip: The cookie-cutter rule: validity is about the shape of the cutter (the logical structure), not the flavour of the dough (whether the individual facts are true). items.stem: "Running a country is just like running a household budget — you can't spend more than you earn." What is the main weakness of this analogy?

choices.text: Households never have any debt.

items.stem: A journalist interviews five people leaving a luxury car dealership and concludes "most people in this city are wealthy." The main problem with this conclusion is:

choices.text: Five people is an unbiased, representative sample of the city.
The sample is both too small and drawn from a location (a luxury dealership) that is not representative of the general population.

Memory tip: Check both SIZE and SOURCE: a shaky sample can fail because it's too SIZE-small, drawn from the wrong SOURCE (a biased subgroup), or both — GAMSAT often hides one while flaunting the other. Memory tip: "Top and bottom": a rate is a fraction. Before trusting any "the rate went up/down" claim, ask what moved on top (the numerator) and what moved on the bottom (the denominator). items.stem: A population of beetles has varying shell colour. After a change in habitat that increases visibility to predators, darker beetles start being eaten more often. Over many generations, which outcome does natural selection predict?

choices.text: The beetles will consciously evolve to change colour within their own lifetime.

items.explanation: Natural selection acts on existing variation: individuals whose traits improve survival and reproduction (here, lighter colour, better camouflage) leave more offspring, so that trait becomes more frequent in the population over generations — not within one individual's lifetime. No individual organism "evolves" during its own life. Selection changes the frequency of traits across a population over generations, because individuals with advantageous variations survive/reproduce more. Variation must already exist for selection to act on it. Memory tip: "Survival of the fittest population, not the fittest individual's lifetime": no single beetle chooses to lighten up. The population's average colour shifts over generations because lighter beetles out-survive and out-reproduce darker ones. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem: After a meal, blood glucose rises. Insulin is released, causing cells to take up glucose and lowering blood sugar back toward normal. This is an example of:

choices.text: Positive feedback, amplifying the original change.
Negative feedback, counteracting the original change to restore a stable set point.
A one-way, non-regulated process.
An immune response.

items.explanation: The rise in glucose triggers a response (insulin release) that pushes glucose back down — the response opposes the original change, which is the hallmark of negative feedback. Most homeostatic systems (blood sugar, body temperature, blood pressure) use negative feedback: a deviation from the set point triggers a corrective response in the opposite direction. Positive feedback (e.g. childbirth contractions, blood clotting) instead amplifies change — much rarer in the body. Memory tip: Thermostat rule: negative feedback works like a thermostat correcting back toward a set point (blood sugar too high -> insulin brings it down). Positive feedback is the rare exception that amplifies change, like a snowball rolling downhill (e.g. childbirth contractions). Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem: An atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons, and is neutral. How many electrons does it have?
items.explanation: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. Protons = 17, so electrons = 17 (neutrons don't affect charge or electron count). Memory tip: Protons are your passport — they define your identity (the element) and never change without you becoming a different element. items.stem: Moving left to right across a period (row) of the periodic table, atomic radius generally:

choices.text: Increases, because more electrons take up more space.
Decreases, because increasing nuclear charge pulls the same electron shell in more tightly.

Down a group: an extra electron shell is added each row, with inner electrons shielding the pull -> radius grows, ionisation energy falls. Learn the "why" (charge vs shielding) rather than memorising each trend separately. Memory tip: Picture the nucleus in a tug of war with its electrons: across a period, more protons pull the SAME shell in tighter (radius shrinks); down a group, a whole new outer shell is added each row, further from the pull (radius grows). This single rule predicts bond type for most GAMSAT-level compounds. Memory tip: "Metals give, non-metals share": a metal + non-metal pairing means one atom GIVES away an electron (ionic bond); two non-metals SHARE electrons because neither wants to give theirs up (covalent bond). Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem: A fixed amount of gas is heated at constant volume. What happens to its pressure, and why?

Memory tip: Picture gas particles as tiny tennis balls bouncing off the container walls: heat them up and they slam the walls faster and more often — "faster particles hit harder," which is why pressure rises. items.stem: For the equilibrium N2 + 3H2 2NH3 (exothermic forward reaction), what happens if the temperature is increased?

choices.text: The equilibrium shifts toward the products (more NH3) to absorb the extra heat.

For temperature specifically, treat heat like a reactant/product: increasing heat favours whichever direction absorbs heat (the endothermic direction). Memory tip: "The system pushes back": treat added heat like an extra ingredient on whichever side absorbs it (the endothermic direction), and picture the equilibrium physically leaning away from the stress you applied. passages.title: Critical Reasoning · Philosophy of Science
passages.body: For centuries we have told the story of the solitary genius: Newton alone under his apple tree, Curie alone in her laboratory, the writer alone at her desk producing a masterpiece from nothing but personal brilliance. This narrative is comforting because it is simple, and it sells a great many biographies. It is also, historians of science increasingly argue, badly incomplete. Newton corresponded for decades with a network of mathematicians whose incremental work he built on and later minimised in his own accounts. Curie's laboratory depended on instruments, techniques and a body of prior findings assembled by dozens of researchers across Europe. Even the writer's "original" idea usually turns out, on close inspection, to be a recombination of things read, overheard, or absorbed from a wider culture. None of this makes any of these individuals less remarkable. But it does suggest that crediting a single mind for a breakthrough often erases the scaffolding — the teachers, rivals, funders and quiet collaborators — without which that mind would have had nothing to work with.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption the author relies on but does not explicitly state?

choices.text: Most celebrated individual achievements would have been impossible without prior or contemporaneous input from others.
Newton, Curie and the unnamed writer never contributed anything original of their own.
Biographies about lone geniuses are more commercially successful than accurate ones.
Historians of science are always correct about the individuals they study.

questions.explanation: The author's argument (that crediting one mind "erases the scaffolding") only works if that scaffolding was genuinely necessary to the achievement, not merely present alongside it. That link — between "input existed" and "the achievement depended on it" — is assumed rather than argued for. When a passage moves from "collaborators existed" to "the achievement depended on those collaborators," it is smuggling in an assumption about necessity, not just presence. Ask: what extra premise turns "X was around" into "X was essential"? Memory tip: Same rope-bridge trick as before: find the plank the argument needs but never lays down. Here the plank is "present = necessary" — the author never actually shows the scaffolding was load-bearing, just that it existed. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passages.title: Critical Reasoning · Health & Statistics
passages.body: A widely circulated report claims that teenagers who spend more than four hours a day on social media are twice as likely to report symptoms of anxiety as teenagers who spend less than one hour a day. Newspaper headlines quickly translated this into warnings that social media "causes" anxiety in teenagers, and several schools cited the report when introducing new phone bans. The original researchers were more cautious. They noted that their data was cross-sectional — collected at a single point in time — rather than following the same teenagers over years, and that anxious teenagers might simply be more likely to retreat into their phones, rather than phones making them anxious in the first place. They also noted that heavy social media use was more common among teenagers who already reported sleeping fewer than six hours a night, raising the possibility that disrupted sleep, not screen time itself, was doing much of the work.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of using this report to claim that social media causes anxiety?

choices.text: The report did not survey enough teenagers to be statistically meaningful.
The data shows an association at one point in time, and cannot rule out reverse causation or a shared underlying cause such as poor sleep.
Teenagers are unreliable narrators of their own emotional states.
Anxiety cannot be measured using a survey.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly raises two alternative explanations — reverse causation (anxious teens retreat into phones) and a shared cause (poor sleep driving both) — which cross-sectional, single-timepoint data cannot distinguish from social-media-causes-anxiety. A snapshot taken at one moment can show that two things go together, but it cannot show which came first, or whether both are driven by a third factor. Longitudinal data (tracking the same people over time) is needed to start untangling direction and cause. Memory tip: Same puppeteer image, new stage: this time the puppeteer might be poor sleep, or the puppets might even be pulling each other's strings in reverse (anxiety causing phone use, not the other way around). A snapshot can't tell you which. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passages.title: Critical Reasoning · Literary Tone & Inference
passages.body: The chair called the meeting to order at exactly nine, though half the room was still finding chairs. She thanked everyone for their punctuality with a smile that did not reach her eyes, then spent the next forty minutes explaining, in exhaustive detail, why the decision that mattered had already been made without them. When someone finally asked a question, she paused just long enough to make the silence uncomfortable before answering it with another question. By the time the meeting closed, three action items had been assigned, none of them to her, and everyone filed out thanking her for her time.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the chair is best described as:

choices.text: Openly admiring and sincere.
Quietly critical, conveyed through irony rather than direct statement.
Completely neutral and factual.
Overtly hostile and insulting.

questions.explanation: The details — a smile that "did not reach her eyes," a pause designed to make silence uncomfortable, work assigned to everyone but herself — build a critical portrait without the author ever stating "the chair was manipulative" outright. That is irony, not neutral reporting or open hostility. Tone can build up across several small, carefully chosen details rather than one obvious clue. Add them up before judging tone — no single sentence here is hostile, but the pattern across all four is unmistakably critical. Memory tip: Death by a thousand details: no single sentence insults the chair, but stack four small unflattering details and the sarcastic verdict writes itself. Look for the pattern, not a single smoking gun. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passages.title: Critical Reasoning · Environmental Policy
passages.body: Beekeepers in the region have reported that average honey yields per hive fell by 30% over the past five years, and several have linked this decline to the increased use of a new class of pesticide introduced during the same period. Advocacy groups have used the honey yield figures to call for an immediate ban. Agricultural researchers point out that the same five years also saw two unusually dry summers and a rise in a parasitic mite known to weaken hive productivity independently of pesticide exposure. A separate long-term study, tracking the same hives annually since before the pesticide was introduced, found no significant difference in yield decline between hives in treated and untreated areas.

Beekeepers are not qualified to measure honey yields accurately.
Advocacy groups should not be allowed to comment on scientific matters.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly names two alternative, independent causes of hive productivity decline occurring over the same window, which the raw yield figures alone cannot rule out as explanations instead of the pesticide. When several plausible causes change at the same time as the outcome, blaming any one of them requires evidence that isolates its specific contribution — simply pointing at the timeline is not enough. Memory tip: Three suspects, one crime scene: pesticide, drought and mites were all present when yields fell. Naming just one as guilty needs evidence that rules out the other two, not just proof it was in the room. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passages.title: Biology · Gene Regulation
passages.body: A research group is studying a heat-shock protein gene, HSP-70X, thought to help wheat seedlings survive short bursts of extreme heat. They suspect a regulatory protein, called ReguFactor B, switches HSP-70X on when temperatures rise. To test this, they create three groups of genetically modified wheat seedlings: one where ReguFactor B is overexpressed (produced in excess), one where the gene for ReguFactor B is knocked out (disabled), and a normal (wild-type) control group. All seedlings are exposed to a two-hour heat spike, and HSP-70X mRNA levels are measured immediately afterwards. The overexpression group shows HSP-70X mRNA levels roughly four times higher than the wild-type control. The knockout group shows almost no detectable HSP-70X mRNA at all, even after the heat spike. Under normal, non-heat conditions, HSP-70X mRNA levels are low and roughly equal across all three groups.

questions.stem: Based on the results, what is the most likely role of ReguFactor B in regulating HSP-70X expression during heat stress?

choices.text: ReguFactor B has no effect on HSP-70X expression.
ReguFactor B acts as a repressor, blocking HSP-70X expression during heat stress.
ReguFactor B acts as an activator, switching on HSP-70X expression during heat stress.
ReguFactor B degrades HSP-70X mRNA after heat stress.

questions.explanation: Overexpressing ReguFactor B increases HSP-70X mRNA (more activator → more activation), while knocking it out almost eliminates HSP-70X mRNA even under heat stress (no activator → no activation). Both results point the same direction: ReguFactor B switches HSP-70X ON. Overexpression and knockout results are two ends of the same lever — if more of a regulator means more of the target gene's expression, and less of the regulator means less expression, the regulator is an activator. If the pattern were reversed, it would be a repressor. Memory tip: "Push up, push down": if pushing the regulator up pushes the target up, and pushing it down pushes the target down, they're moving together — that's an activator, not a repressor (which would move the target the opposite way). Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

questions.stem: Which of the following conclusions would NOT be justified by this experiment alone?

choices.text: ReguFactor B increases HSP-70X mRNA levels specifically under heat stress.
Knocking out ReguFactor B nearly eliminates the heat-induced rise in HSP-70X mRNA.
ReguFactor B is the only factor capable of regulating HSP-70X in any species of plant.
Overexpressing ReguFactor B increases HSP-70X mRNA roughly four-fold compared to wild-type.

questions.explanation: The experiment tested only wheat seedlings and only this one regulatory protein, so it cannot support a sweeping claim about the "only" factor or about "any species." A, B and D are direct, specific readouts of the described data; C over-generalises far beyond a single-species, single-gene study. A result is only justified for the specific conditions actually tested. Watch for answer choices that use words like "only," "always," or "any" — they usually extrapolate beyond what a single, narrowly-scoped experiment can support. Memory tip: "One trial, one species, one claim": a red flag word like "only" or "any" in an answer choice should make you check whether the experiment actually tested that broadly — here, it tested one gene in one crop. passages.title: Chemistry · Enzyme Kinetics
passages.body: A student investigates how temperature affects the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction, using an enzyme called amylase to break down starch into sugar. They measure the time taken for a fixed amount of starch to be fully broken down at five different temperatures: 10°C, 20°C, 30°C, 40°C and 50°C, keeping the amylase concentration and starch concentration constant in every trial. The reaction is fastest at 40°C. At 50°C, the reaction is slower than at 40°C, and even slower than at 30°C, despite the higher temperature. At 10°C, the reaction is very slow but still eventually completes.

questions.stem: What does the pattern of results across all five temperatures suggest about amylase's relationship with temperature?

choices.text: Reaction rate increases steadily with temperature with no limit.
Amylase has an optimal temperature (around 40°C) beyond which rate decreases, consistent with denaturation at higher temperatures.
Temperature has no effect on amylase activity.
Amylase works fastest at the lowest temperature tested.

questions.explanation: Rate rises from 10°C to a peak at 40°C, then falls at 50°C — a classic optimum-temperature curve, consistent with the enzyme beginning to denature once temperature climbs past its ideal range. Reaction rate rises with temperature only up to a point, because higher temperature also risks denaturing the enzyme. Past the optimum, the denaturation effect outweighs the speed benefit, and rate falls even though the temperature is higher. Memory tip: Picture an upside-down U on a graph, not a straight uphill line — rate climbs, peaks, then drops as heat starts wrecking the enzyme's shape. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

questions.stem: What is the most likely explanation for the reaction being slower at 50°C than at 40°C, despite 50°C being the higher temperature?

choices.text: There was less starch available at 50°C.
The higher temperature likely began denaturing the amylase, disrupting its active site and reducing its ability to bind starch.
Amylase works better in cold conditions in general.
The timer used to measure the reaction was faulty only at 50°C.

questions.explanation: Since starch and amylase concentrations were held constant across all trials, the drop in rate at 50°C is best explained by heat-induced denaturation disrupting the enzyme's active site, not by a change in the amount of substrate or a measurement fault. Denaturation does not remove the enzyme molecules — it distorts their 3D shape, especially the active site, so they can no longer bind their substrate effectively. The enzyme is still present, just non-functional. Memory tip: Same wax-figure image as before: the amylase is still physically there at 50°C, it's just melted out of the shape it needs to grip starch. questions.stem: Which of the following was deliberately kept constant across all five trials, allowing temperature’s effect to be isolated?

choices.text: The temperature of each trial.
The time taken for the reaction to complete.
The concentration of amylase and starch used in each trial.
The identity of the enzyme used across different trials.

questions.explanation: The passage states that amylase and starch concentrations were kept constant in every trial. This is what makes it possible to attribute any change in reaction rate specifically to the one variable that was deliberately changed — temperature — rather than to some other difference between trials. A fair test changes only one variable at a time while holding everything else constant. If concentration also varied between trials, you would not be able to tell whether temperature or concentration caused any observed change in rate. Memory tip: "One dial at a time": if you only turn the temperature dial and leave every other dial fixed, any change in outcome can only be blamed on the dial you turned. passages.title: Physics · Pendulum Motion & Energy
passages.body: A student sets up a pendulum using a string and a small metal bob, and investigates what affects the time for one complete swing (the period). They test three string lengths (25 cm, 50 cm, 100 cm) while keeping the bob's mass and the release angle constant, and separately test three different bob masses (10 g, 50 g, 100 g) while keeping the string length and release angle constant. Increasing the string length increases the period. Changing the bob's mass, however, produces no measurable change in the period. In a separate trial, the student releases the pendulum from a fixed height and measures its speed at the lowest point of the swing using a sensor, finding that the speed is slightly lower on each successive swing as the pendulum gradually loses height.

questions.stem: In the first part of the experiment (testing string length), which variable was deliberately controlled?

choices.text: String length.
The bob's mass and the release angle.
The period of the pendulum.
The material the string was made of.

questions.explanation: The passage states mass and release angle were kept constant while string length was varied, meaning mass and release angle are the controlled variables, string length is the tested (independent) variable, and period is the measured (dependent) variable. In a fair test: the independent variable is what you deliberately change, the dependent variable is what you measure as a result, and controlled variables are everything else you deliberately hold constant so they cannot explain the result instead. Memory tip: "Change one, measure one, freeze the rest": string length changes, period is measured, mass and angle are frozen — three roles, three variables, don't mix them up. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

questions.stem: What is the most reasonable conclusion from the finding that changing the bob's mass produced no measurable change in the period?

choices.text: The experiment was flawed and should be discarded.
Within the range tested, the pendulum's period does not depend on the mass of the bob.
Heavier bobs always swing faster than lighter ones.
Mass cannot be measured accurately using standard laboratory equipment.

questions.explanation: A "no effect" result is itself informative: it supports the conclusion that, across the masses actually tested, period does not depend on mass. There is no basis in the passage for concluding the experiment was flawed or that mass cannot be measured. Finding that a variable has no measurable effect is a legitimate scientific finding, not evidence of a failed experiment. Don't assume something went wrong just because the result was "nothing happened" — sometimes nothing happening is the answer. Memory tip: "No effect is still an answer": a flat line on a graph is data too, not a broken experiment — don't throw out a null result just because it isn't exciting. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

questions.stem: Why does the pendulum's speed at the lowest point of the swing decrease slightly on each successive swing?

choices.text: Kinetic energy is being converted into potential energy with no loss.
Some mechanical energy is being lost to air resistance and friction (e.g. at the string's pivot), converting into heat rather than being conserved as motion.
The pendulum's mass is decreasing over time.
Gravity becomes weaker with each swing.

questions.explanation: In a real (non-ideal) system, air resistance and pivot friction convert some mechanical energy into heat on every swing, so both the height reached and the speed at the bottom gradually decrease. Mass and gravity do not change during the experiment. In an idealised frictionless system, total mechanical energy is perfectly conserved. In any real system, some energy always leaks out as heat via friction or air resistance, which is why a real pendulum (or swing, or rollercoaster) gradually loses height over time. Memory tip: "Energy changes outfits, and loses a sock each time": each swing still converts potential to kinetic energy and back, but a little energy quietly slips away as heat via friction — that's the missing sock. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passages.title: Biology · Exercise Physiology
passages.body: Researchers measure blood lactate concentration in athletes performing exercise at increasing intensity on a stationary bike. At low to moderate intensity, blood lactate stays low and roughly stable. Above a certain intensity — different for each athlete, but typically around 70–80% of their maximum effort — blood lactate concentration begins rising sharply and continues to climb the longer the athlete sustains that intensity. Athletes who report more years of endurance training tend to reach this "lactate threshold" at a higher percentage of their maximum effort than less-trained athletes.

questions.stem: What is the most likely explanation for blood lactate rising sharply above a certain exercise intensity?

choices.text: Above that intensity, the muscles' demand for energy outpaces the oxygen supply, so a growing share of energy production shifts to anaerobic respiration, which produces lactate as a byproduct.
Lactate is produced only when muscles stop working entirely.
Aerobic respiration produces more lactate than anaerobic respiration.
Blood lactate rises independently of exercise intensity.

questions.explanation: As intensity rises, oxygen delivery eventually cannot keep pace with muscle energy demand, forcing a shift toward anaerobic respiration, which produces lactate as a byproduct — explaining why lactate rises sharply only above a threshold intensity, not at low intensity. The body defaults to efficient aerobic respiration when oxygen supply can meet demand. Once demand outpaces supply, cells increasingly rely on faster but less efficient anaerobic respiration, which is why lactate (its byproduct) only accumulates sharply past a certain effort level. Memory tip: "Oxygen can't keep up, so the body switches lanes": below threshold, oxygen supply matches demand (aerobic lane); above it, demand outruns supply and the body merges into the anaerobic lane, producing lactate as the toll. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

questions.stem: What is the most reasonable explanation for why more highly trained endurance athletes reach their lactate threshold at a higher percentage of maximum effort?

choices.text: Trained athletes' muscles and cardiovascular systems are likely better able to supply and use oxygen at higher intensities, delaying the shift toward anaerobic respiration.
Trained athletes do not produce lactate at all.
Training makes muscles heavier, which lowers the intensity needed to reach the threshold.
The lactate threshold is unrelated to oxygen supply.

questions.explanation: Since the lactate threshold is explained by oxygen supply failing to meet demand, a trained athlete reaching threshold later (at higher relative intensity) is best explained by an improved capacity to supply and use oxygen, delaying the point at which anaerobic respiration must take over. When a passage gives you a mechanism for a phenomenon, use that same mechanism to explain differences between groups, rather than inventing an unrelated new explanation. The strongest answer usually extends the logic already established, not a new one. Memory tip: "Same engine, better fuel line": training doesn't change the underlying mechanism (oxygen vs anaerobic switch) — it just improves how much oxygen can be delivered before the switch has to happen. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

questions.stem: Two athletes exercise at exactly 75% of their own individual maximum effort. Athlete X is highly trained; Athlete Y is untrained. Based on the passage, which athlete is more likely to already be past their lactate threshold at this intensity?

choices.text: Athlete X, because trained athletes reach threshold at a lower percentage of effort.
Athlete Y, because untrained athletes reach their lactate threshold at a lower percentage of maximum effort, so 75% is more likely to already be above their threshold.
Both athletes will have identical lactate levels regardless of training.
Neither athlete can reach a lactate threshold.

questions.explanation: Since untrained athletes reach their lactate threshold at a lower percentage of maximum effort (per the passage), Athlete Y is more likely to have already crossed their threshold at 75%, while trained Athlete X's higher threshold means they may still be below it at the same relative intensity. Once a passage establishes a general relationship (here, training level vs threshold percentage), you should be able to apply it to predict a new, specific case not explicitly described. This tests whether you understood the relationship well enough to use it, not just recall it. Memory tip: "Same number, different meaning": 75% means something different for each athlete because their thresholds sit at different points — don't treat the number as identical just because it looks identical.
